gains.label: 1 day
gains.title: The tough patch starts
gains.body: Within about a day you may feel irritable, restless, anxious or low, and find it harder to concentrate. These are recognised withdrawal effects, not a sign you are failing.
gains.work: Front-load your hardest thinking to the morning, keep meetings light where you can, and warn a colleague you might be short-tempered this week.
gains.note: Symptoms and intensity vary a lot between people; stop-smoking medicines can soften them.

gains.label: 2 days
gains.title: Sleep may be choppy for a while
gains.body: In a sleep-lab study, people woke more and spent more of the night awake in the first days without nicotine. Broken sleep can make the next day feel foggier.
gains.work: Protect your sleep window, skip caffeine after lunch, and do not judge your focus on a day after a bad night.
gains.note: Small study (33 smokers), measured at 24-36 hours. Exactly how long sleep disruption lasts was not clear from what we could read; weeks rather than days is a reasoned guess.

gains.label: 3 days
gains.title: Working memory may dip
gains.body: Abstinence studies find smokers often do worse on working-memory and attention tasks in early withdrawal. The first few days are usually the hardest.
gains.work: Write things down instead of holding them in your head, use checklists, and break big tasks into 25-minute blocks with short walks between.
gains.note: Placing the peak around days 2-4 is our reasoned estimate from general withdrawal research. This study found the dip was smaller in smokers aged 50+.

gains.label: 5 days
gains.title: The 'calming' cigarette, explained
gains.body: Research suggests the calm a cigarette seemed to give was mostly relief from withdrawal tension that built up since the last one. Once withdrawal fades, that tension cycle tends to fade too.
gains.work: When a work stress spike hits, try a 2-minute breathing break or a short walk instead; the urge usually passes within minutes.
gains.note: This is an explanatory model supported by mood-pattern studies, not a single measured milestone; the day-5 placement is ours.

gains.label: 3 weeks
gains.title: Concentration and mood start to settle
gains.body: For most people, irritability, restlessness and poor concentration ease over roughly the first two to four weeks. Cravings can linger longer but tend to get less frequent.
gains.work: This is a good point to schedule demanding projects again, while keeping a plan for the occasional strong craving at stressful moments.
gains.note: The two-to-four-week range is widely cited; we could not confirm the exact figure from the review's abstract, so treat it as approximate.

gains.label: 1 month
gains.title: Day-to-day stress tends to fall
gains.body: People who stayed quit reported lower perceived stress over the following months, while those who went back to smoking reported more. Many quitters expect the opposite.
gains.work: Notice whether hard workdays feel a little more manageable now; jotting a weekly stress score can make the change visible.
gains.note: Stress was measured at 1, 3 and 6 months. Observational, so lower stress may partly help people stay quit rather than only result from it.

gains.label: 6 weeks
gains.title: Brain nicotine receptors head back to normal
gains.body: Brain scans showed nicotine receptors were raised at 1 week of abstinence but no longer different from non-smokers by about 4 weeks, and still normal at 6-12 weeks.
gains.work: If cravings feel weaker in meetings or on deadlines around now, this rebalancing may be part of why.
gains.sourceName: Cosgrove et al. 2009, Archives of General Psychiatry
gains.note: Small SPECT study (about 19 smokers). Linking receptor levels to how you feel is plausible but not proven.

gains.label: 6 weeks
gains.title: Less anxiety, depression and stress
gains.body: Across studies, people who quit had lower anxiety, depression and stress and better positive mood than those who kept smoking, measured from six weeks onward. This held for people with mental health conditions too.
gains.work: Expect your baseline mood on long days to be steadier than in the first weeks; a calmer baseline can make it easier to handle pressure.
gains.note: Meta-analysis of observational data, so cause and effect is not certain; other lifestyle changes may contribute.

gains.label: 2 months
gains.title: Wellbeing and quality of life
gains.body: A large Cochrane review found quitting was linked to small to moderate improvements in mood and anxiety, and found no sign that quitting harms mental health.
gains.work: Reinvest the time once spent on smoke breaks in short movement or social breaks; they help mood and keep you fresh through the afternoon.
gains.sourceName: Taylor et al. 2021, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
gains.note: Certainty ranged from very low to moderate. The 2-month placement is ours; the studies covered a range of follow-up times.

gains.label: 3 months
gains.title: Reward system may rebalance
gains.body: One brain-imaging study found smokers made less dopamine in a reward area than non-smokers, and this appeared to normalise after about three months without smoking.
gains.work: Everyday rewards, like finishing a task or a good coffee, may start to feel more satisfying; use them deliberately to mark progress at work.
gains.note: Small PET study of men only; 15 quitters re-scanned and some regional analyses had fewer. Needs replication.

gains.label: 6 months
gains.title: Anxiety lower than if you had relapsed
gains.body: In a UK cohort, anxiety fell over six months in people who stayed quit and rose in those who relapsed. The fall was largest in people who had smoked to cope.
gains.work: If you used cigarettes to get through stressful days, this is encouraging: you may handle pressure better without them over time.
gains.sourceName: McDermott et al. 2013, British Journal of Psychiatry

gains.label: 1 year
gains.title: Brain blood flow may improve
gains.body: An older study found blood flow to the brain rose steadily over the first year after quitting, while it did not change in people who kept smoking.
gains.work: Better circulation supports a healthy brain long term; pair it with regular movement away from the desk for the most benefit.
gains.note: Dated method; later small studies are mixed and some find regional differences persist in ex-smokers. Carbon monoxide in the blood clears much sooner, within hours to days.

gains.label: 2 years
gains.title: Brain's outer layer may slowly recover
gains.body: Smoking is linked to a thinner cortex. In older adults, former smokers' cortex looked partly recovered for each smoke-free year, though full recovery appeared to take decades.
gains.work: This is a slow, long-term payoff; each smoke-free year likely counts, so a slip is worth getting straight back from.
gains.note: Cross-sectional study of 504 people aged 73, so recovery is inferred, not tracked. The 2-year placement is ours to show a gradual effect.

gains.label: 5 years
gains.title: Lower dementia risk than if you smoked on
gains.body: In a large Korean study of men over 60, long-term quitters had a modestly lower risk of dementia than men who kept smoking.
gains.work: Quitting is one of the clearer steps you can take now to protect your thinking for later working years and retirement.
gains.sourceName: Choi et al. 2018, Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology
gains.note: Observational, men only, about 8 years of follow-up, no education data. The 5-year placement is our reading of 'long-term quitters'.

gains.label: 10 years
gains.title: Slower thinking decline with age
gains.body: In the Whitehall II study, men who kept smoking showed faster cognitive decline, while men quit for 10+ years did not decline faster than never-smokers.
gains.work: Over a career, this is about keeping memory and reasoning sharper for longer, not about being sharper tomorrow.
gains.sourceName: Sabia et al. 2012, Archives of General Psychiatry
gains.note: Observational; the effect was seen in men but not women, possibly because the men smoked more. Recent quitters still showed some extra decline.

caveats: Nicotine is a mild short-term stimulant, so quitting will not make you smarter; the honest story is that the early dip passes and long-term brain and mental health tend to be better.
Timings are typical averages from studies, many of them observational, and your own experience may be faster or slower.
If you have a history of depression or another mental health condition, watch your mood closely and involve your doctor, who can also adjust any medication affected by quitting.
Stop-smoking medicines and support services can make the first weeks easier and improve your chances of staying quit.
